pos: n. (archiepiscopal see and university city of Sweden; where the Assembly of 1593 bound the realm to the Augsburg Confession)
etymology: From Old Norse Uppsalir, the upper halls; upp, up, and salir, halls.
biblical_def: Uppsala is where Sweden decided what it believed. The archbishopric was founded in 1164 and the university in 1477, and the city had been the centre of Swedish heathen worship before either. The Reformation came to it slowly and from the crown, and for sixty years the Swedish church had evangelical practice without an agreed confession. That was settled at the Uppsala Assembly in February 1593, when the clergy and estates, facing the accession of the Roman Catholic Sigismund, adopted the unaltered Augsburg Confession, the three ancient creeds and the Swedish church ordinance, and declared that no other doctrine would be tolerated in the realm. Sigismund was eventually deposed. The dictionary records Uppsala because a church that will not state its confession cannot resist a king who has one. Paul asks of a congregation exactly what the Swedes finally did, “that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel” (Php 1:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession as a formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; unity as the state of being one, concord, agreement; and an assembly as a company of persons collected together in one place.
webster_full: CONFESSION, n. [L. confessio.] A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a public avowal of one's belief.
UNITY, n. [L. unitas.] The state of being one; oneness; concord; conjunction; agreement; uniformity.
ASSEMBLY, n. A company or collection of individuals in the same place, usually for the same purpose.
TOLERATE, v.t. [L. tolero.] To suffer to be or to be done without prohibition or hindrance; to allow or permit negatively.
scriptures: Php 1:27

Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Eph 4:5
One Lord, one faith, one baptism,
Act 4:32
And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.
corruption_summary: Sweden's archiepiscopal see and university; the Assembly of 1593 bound the realm to the Augsburg Confession against a Catholic king.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is confessional indifference presented as breadth. A church that declines to say where its boundaries lie has not become generous; it has become indefensible, and the first determined party to arrive will define it instead. Sweden ran that experiment for sixty years and nearly lost the Reformation to a single royal succession. The opposite error, a confession held as a party badge without being understood or taught, is equally barren, and Sweden later suffered that too.

The principle to recover is that doctrinal agreement is commanded, not merely hoped for. Paul beseeches the Corinthians “that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10), and he grounds church unity in objective singulars rather than in goodwill: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph 4:5). The first church is described in the same terms of mind and affection, for they “were of one heart and of one soul” (Act 4:32).

“that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) — the unaltered Augsburg Confession adopted.
“One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph 4:5) — archbishopric from 1164, university from 1477.

pos: n. (city and see of central Sweden; where the Diet of 1527 transferred the church's property to the crown)
etymology: From Swedish Västerås, contracted from Västra Årós, the western river mouth.
biblical_def: Vasteras gave the Swedish Reformation its legal foundation and its permanent ambiguity. At the Diet held there in June 1527, Gustav Vasa told the estates he would abdicate unless they relieved his treasury, and they voted him the surplus revenues and much of the landed property of the church, permitted the preaching of the gospel, and allowed the bishops to be appointed without papal confirmation. No doctrine was defined. The crown got the estates, the preachers got liberty, and the question of what the Swedish church actually taught was left open for sixty-six years until Uppsala settled it. The dictionary records the Diet because it shows the Reformation and the plundering of the church arriving in the same instrument, which neither excuses the plundering nor discredits the preaching. Our Lord gives the only safe rule about ecclesiastical wealth, and He gives it as a command: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt” (Mat 6:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines treasure as wealth accumulated, riches hoarded; a diet as an assembly of princes or estates; and to covet as to desire inordinately, to desire what belongs to another.
webster_full: TREASURE, n. [L. thesaurus.] Wealth accumulated; particularly, a stock or store of money in reserve; great abundance of riches.
DIET, n. [Low L. dieta.] An assembly of princes or delegates for the discussion and decision of political affairs; a convention.
COVET, v.t. [L. cupio.] To desire inordinately; to desire that which it is unlawful to obtain or possess.
SACRILEGE, n. [L. sacrilegium.] The crime of violating or profaning sacred things; the alienating to common purposes what has been devoted to religion.
scriptures: Mat 6:19
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
Mat 6:20
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
Act 3:6
Then Peter said, Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk.
corruption_summary: The Diet of 1527 gave Gustav Vasa the church's property and the preachers their liberty, and defined no doctrine at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions are visible at Vasteras and the dictionary names both. The first is the medieval accumulation that made the seizure possible: a church holding a fifth of a kingdom's land had long since stopped being able to preach against covetousness. The second is the crown's, which took the lands and gave the church no confession in exchange, so that for two generations the Swedish church had freedom without a definition and depended on the goodwill of whoever wore the crown.

The principle to recover is that the church's wealth is a danger to it and that its real strength lies elsewhere. Christ sets the alternative treasury against the earthly one: “But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt” (Mat 6:20). Paul traces apostasy itself to the love of money, “For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10), by which some have erred from the faith. And Peter at the temple gate shows what a poor church can still do: “Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee” (Act 3:6).

pos: n. (town of central Sweden; site of the national synod of 1529, the first of the Swedish Reformation)
etymology: From Swedish Örebro, the bridge over the gravel ford; ör, gravel, and bro, bridge.
biblical_def: The Synod of Orebro in February 1529 was the Swedish church's first attempt to say what should change and what might stay. Laurentius Andreae presided and Olaus Petri was its working theologian, and its decisions were cautious to a degree that has disappointed every later party: preaching was required in every parish and the Scriptures were to be read in the schools; the old ceremonies were not abolished but were to be explained, so that the people would understand that they did not save; feast days were pruned; the saints' days were retained with the saints presented as examples rather than intercessors. A rising in Vastergotland the same year showed what a faster pace would have cost. The dictionary records Orebro because it is a careful instance of a hard pastoral question: how fast may a church be reformed when the people do not yet understand the reformation. Paul's rule governs it: “Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations” (Rom 14:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a ceremony as an outward rite, external form in religion; a synod as an ecclesiastical council; and weak as feeble, infirm, and figuratively wanting moral or spiritual strength.
webster_full: CEREMONY, n. [L. caeremonia.] Outward rite; external form in religion; the forms of civility; outward forms of state.
SYNOD, n. [Gr. an assembly.] A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
WEAK, adj. Feeble; infirm; not strong; wanting spirit; wanting moral or spiritual strength.
EDIFICATION, n. Improvement; instruction; the building up of the mind in knowledge and grace.
scriptures: Rom 14:1
Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
Rom 14:5
One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak.
Rom 15:1
We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves.
corruption_summary: Sweden's first Reformation synod, 1529, which required preaching everywhere and explained the old ceremonies rather than abolishing them.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the use of forbearance as a cover for permanence, so that ceremonies retained for a season because the people were not ready are still there three centuries later with the reason forgotten. Sweden kept more of the medieval ceremonial than any other Reformation church and has had to argue about it ever since. The opposite corruption is impatience, which reforms a parish faster than it can teach it and leaves a congregation stripped of what it had and ignorant of what replaced it.

The principle to recover is the care of the weak conscience during change, without surrendering the goal of the change. Paul allows real difference of judgment in things not commanded, “Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” (Rom 14:5), and warns the strong against pressing their liberty, “take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak” (1Co 8:9). The duty falls on the stronger party: “We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves” (Rom 15:1).

pos: n. (capital of Sweden; where Olaus Petri preached and the Swedish Bible of 1541 was prepared)
etymology: From Swedish Stockholm, the log islet; stock, a log or pile, and holme, an islet.
biblical_def: Stockholm was the pulpit of the Swedish Reformation. In November 1520 it was the scene of the bloodbath in which Christian II of Denmark executed some eighty Swedish nobles and churchmen after promising amnesty, an act that destroyed Danish rule in Sweden and put Gustav Vasa on the throne. Under the new king, Olaus Petri became preacher and then pastor at the Great Church of the city, and from Stockholm came the Swedish New Testament of 1526, the Swedish manual and mass, and in 1541 the complete Swedish Bible, the Gustav Vasa Bible, translated under Laurentius Petri and printed at Uppsala. The dictionary records the city because a Bible and a massacre came out of the same decade and the same place, and only one of them is still doing anything. Scripture requires the king himself to be a reader of it: “he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God” (Deu 17:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a copy as a writing like another writing, a transcript; certainty as a full assurance of mind, exemption from doubt; and to instruct as to teach, to inform the mind.
webster_full: COPY, n. [L. copia.] A writing like another writing; a transcript from an original; hence, a book or writing of any kind.
CERTAINTY, n. [L. certus.] A fixed and real state; full assurance of mind; exemption from doubt.
INSTRUCT, v.t. [L. instruo.] To teach; to inform the mind; to communicate knowledge to.
VERSION, n. [L. versio.] A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
scriptures: And it shall be, when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write him a copy of this law in a book out of that which is before the priests the Levites:
And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them:
But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.
Luk 1:4
That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.
corruption_summary: Scene of the 1520 bloodbath and of Olaus Petri's pulpit; the Swedish New Testament of 1526 and the Bible of 1541 came from here.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The nearer error is the reading of the Swedish Reformation as nothing but statecraft, a king's instrument against Denmark and against the bishops. The politics were real and often sordid. But the New Testament of 1526 was translated, printed and read, and no account of national interest explains why a people kept reading it for four centuries after the dynastic quarrel was settled.

The principle to recover is that Scripture is given to produce certainty, and that it was written for that purpose. Moses required the king to write out a copy for himself, “that he shall write him a copy of this law in a book” (Deu 17:18), so that the man with the most power would be the man most under the text. John states the aim of his own Gospel plainly: “But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (Joh 20:31). Luke writes so that a reader already taught may be sure of it, “That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” (Luk 1:4).

roots_lines: Hebrew mishneh (H4932) — a double, a copy, a second; Deuteronomy 17:18.
Greek asphaleia (G803) — firmness, certainty, safety; Luke 1:4.
Hebrew qara (H7121) — to call, to read aloud, to proclaim; Deuteronomy 17:19.

“But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (Joh 20:31) — the Gustav Vasa Bible, 1541.

pos: n. (cathedral city of Sodermanland, Sweden; where Gustav Vasa was elected king in 1523 and where the Swedish Reformation began)
etymology: From Swedish Strängnäs, the headland by the strand; ström or stränd, and näs, a promontory.
biblical_def: Strangnas is where the Swedish Reformation acquired its two men. The cathedral chapter there held Laurentius Andreae as archdeacon and Olaus Petri as deacon and schoolmaster, both evangelical, the one a statesman and the other a theologian; and at the diet held in the town on 6 June 1523 Gustav Vasa was elected king of Sweden, with Andreae at once becoming his chancellor. From that single chapter came the king's ecclesiastical policy, the Swedish New Testament, the Swedish mass and manual, and the arguments that carried the Diet of Vasteras. Olaus Petri's brother Laurentius Petri, later the first evangelical archbishop, was also of the circle. The dictionary records Strangnas because reformations are usually the work of small groups of men who happen to be in the same place, and Scripture does not treat that as an accident. “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecc 4:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chapter as a society of clergymen belonging to a cathedral; a cord as a string or small rope of several strands; and agreed as settled by consent, being in concord.
webster_full: CHAPTER, n. [L. capitulum.] A society of clergymen belonging to a cathedral or collegiate church; the body of canons.
CORD, n. [L. chorda.] A string, or small rope, composed of several strands twisted together.
AGREE, v.i. [Fr. agreer.] To be of one mind; to harmonize in opinion; to live in concord.
CHANCELLOR, n. A high judicial or administrative officer; in some states, the keeper of the seals.
scriptures: Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
Ecc 4:12
And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
Amo 3:3
Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
Mar 6:7
And he called unto him the twelve, and began to send them forth by two and two; and gave them power over unclean spirits;
corruption_summary: The cathedral chapter that held Laurentius Andreae and Olaus Petri; Gustav Vasa was elected king in the town, 6 June 1523.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error nearer at hand is the cult of the solitary reformer, which makes a movement the achievement of one great man and so excuses everyone who is not one. Luther had Melanchthon and Bugenhagen; Calvin had Farel, Viret and Beza; Sweden had a chapter of three or four men in a provincial cathedral town. None of them worked alone, and the pairing was not incidental to what they accomplished.

The principle to recover is that God ordinarily sends men out in company and that agreement precedes usefulness. The preacher gives the reason in a figure, that “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecc 4:12). Amos puts the prior requirement as a question with one answer: “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3). And Christ Himself adopted the pattern when He sent out the twelve, for He “began to send them forth by two and two” (Mar 6:7).

Hebrew chut (H2339) — a thread, a cord, a line; Ecclesiastes 4:12.

Hebrew sakar (H7939) — wages, hire, reward; Ecclesiastes 4:9.

“Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3) — Gustav Vasa elected king here, 6 June 1523.
“began to send them forth by two and two” (Mar 6:7) — the chancellor and the theologian of the Swedish Reformation.

pos: n. (Swedish bishop-elect of Linkoping, c. 1440–1520; diplomat and soldier, the most political churchman of the pre-Reformation North)
etymology: From Swedish Hemming, a personal name; Gadh, a byname, perhaps from gadd, a sting or goad.
biblical_def: Hemming Gadh was a bishop who spent his life as a soldier and an envoy. Elected to the see of Linkoping, he was never confirmed by Rome despite twenty years of lobbying there, and he turned that energy to Swedish independence instead: he negotiated with Russia against Denmark, raised troops, commanded in the field, and was by common account more effective with a company of men than with a diocese. Taken prisoner by Christian II, he died in Denmark in 1520, the year of the Stockholm bloodbath. He belongs to the old order and not to the Reformation, but he is its necessary prelude, because a church whose bishops were generals and ambassadors had already surrendered the ground on which it might have resisted a reforming king. The dictionary records him as a warning in the apostle's own words: “No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life” (2Ti 2:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to entangle as to involve in difficulties, to perplex; an envoy as a person deputed to transact business with a foreign prince or state; and meekness as softness of temper, mildness, forbearance under injuries.
webster_full: ENTANGLE, v.t. To twist or interweave in such a manner as not to be easily separated; to involve in difficulties; to perplex.
ENVOY, n. [Fr. envoye.] A person deputed by a prince or government to negotiate a treaty or transact other business with a foreign prince or government.
MEEKNESS, n. Softness of temper; mildness; gentleness; forbearance under injuries and provocations.
SOLDIER, n. A man engaged in military service; one whose occupation is military.
scriptures: No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.
And he said unto him, Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?
But thou, O man of God, flee these things; and follow after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, meekness.
Heb 5:4
And no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron.
corruption_summary: Bishop-elect of Linkoping who never held the see, and spent his life as a soldier and envoy for Swedish independence; died a prisoner in 1520.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the political prelate, an office of the medieval church that Rome created and the Reformation did not entirely abolish. Where a bishopric is a seat in the councils of state, the man who wants it will be a politician, and the man who gets it will be judged by political results. Sweden had the type in Hemming Gadh and England in Wolsey; the modern version is the churchman whose public reputation rests on positions that have nothing to do with the gospel.

The principle to recover is that the minister's calling disentangles him from the ordinary business of the world, and that he may not assume an office God has not given. Christ refused a request to arbitrate a family estate, asking “Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?” (Luk 12:14). Paul sets the man of God to pursue other things entirely, “follow after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, meekness” (1Ti 6:11). And Hebrews states the rule for every sacred office: “And no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron” (Heb 5:4).

pos: n. (last Roman Catholic archbishop of Uppsala, 1488–1544; papal legate, historian, and an archbishop who never governed his see)
etymology: Latinised Swedish Månsson; Magnus, great, adopted as a surname by the brothers.
biblical_def: Johannes Magnus was sent to Sweden in 1523 as papal legate to settle the church's affairs and found himself appointed by Gustav Vasa to the vacant archbishopric of Uppsala, which Rome then declined to confirm on the king's terms. He administered the see for a few years, resisted the evangelical drift as far as he could, and in 1526 left the country on an embassy and never returned. He spent his remaining eighteen years in Danzig and Rome, titular archbishop of a Swedish church that had become Lutheran without him, and wrote a history of the kings of the Goths and Swedes which supplied Swedish patriotism with a usable antiquity for two centuries. The dictionary records him because an archbishop in permanent absence is a living illustration of what the shepherd is not. Christ draws the distinction by what each man does when the wolf comes: the hireling “leaveth the sheep, and fleeth” (Joh 10:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hireling as one who serves for wages, and in a bad sense a mercenary; a legate as the pope's ambassador to a prince or state; and a shepherd as one who tends sheep, and figuratively a pastor.
webster_full: HIRELING, n. One who is hired, or who serves for wages; in a bad sense, a mercenary; one who serves for gain without regard to duty.
LEGATE, n. [L. legatus.] An ambassador; particularly, the pope's ambassador to a foreign prince or state.
SHEPHERD, n. A man employed in tending, feeding and guarding sheep; figuratively, a pastor or minister of the gospel.
TITULAR, adj. Existing in title or name only; nominal; having the title without the office or duties.
scriptures: But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep.
The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep.
Eze 34:2

Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD unto the shepherds; Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?
Woe to the idol shepherd that leaveth the flock! the sword shall be upon his arm, and upon his right eye: his arm shall be clean dried up, and his right eye shall be utterly darkened.
corruption_summary: Papal legate made archbishop of Uppsala and never confirmed; left Sweden in 1526 and remained a titular archbishop in exile until 1544.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the benefice held without the duty, which was Rome's standing practice and one of the Reformation's plainest grievances: titles, revenues and jurisdiction attached to men who never saw the flock. Johannes Magnus did not choose his exile and should not be judged as a mere pluralist; but the office he retained for eighteen years in Italy was an office in name only, and the system that allowed it had made the abuse normal.

The principle to recover is that the pastoral office is defined by the feeding and guarding of a particular flock. Christ gives the hireling's motive: “The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep” (Joh 10:13). Ezekiel is sent against shepherds who had inverted the office, “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2). And Zechariah pronounces the sentence on desertion: “Woe to the idol shepherd that leaveth the flock!” (Zec 11:17).

pos: n. (titular archbishop of Uppsala in exile, 1490–1557; author of the History of the Northern Peoples and of the Carta Marina)
etymology: Latinised Swedish Månsson; Olaus, the Latin form of Olof.
biblical_def: Olaus Magnus outlived his brother Johannes and inherited an archbishopric he could not enter. Sent abroad on Swedish business in 1524, he never came home; he spent thirty-three years in Danzig, Venice and Rome, succeeded to the empty title of archbishop of Uppsala in 1544, and turned his exile into scholarship. His Carta Marina of 1539 was the first detailed map of Scandinavia, and his Historia de Gentibus Septentrionalibus of 1555 described the peoples, animals, weather, fishing, mining, warfare and customs of the North in twenty-two books, and was for two hundred years the chief source from which the rest of Europe knew that the North existed. He died in Rome. The dictionary records him because an exile's longing for a country he will not see again is a condition Scripture treats as instructive rather than merely sad: the patriarchs “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an exile as one banished from his country; a pilgrim as a wanderer, a traveller to a distant place; and a stranger as a foreigner, one who belongs to another country.
webster_full: EXILE, n. [L. exilium.] Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country; also, the person banished.
PILGRIM, n. [It. pellegrino.] A wanderer; a traveller; particularly, one who travels to a distance from his own country to visit a holy place.
STRANGER, n. [L. extraneus.] A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one unknown.
CHOROGRAPHY, n. [Gr.] The art or practice of describing particular regions, or the countries of a kingdom.
scriptures: These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
For they that say such things declare plainly that they seek a country.
How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?
Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;
corruption_summary: Titular archbishop of Uppsala from 1544, thirty-three years in exile; his 1555 History of the Northern Peoples taught Europe about the North.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error nearer at hand is the sentimental use of exile as a figure for any discomfort, which empties the word of what the New Testament puts into it. Olaus Magnus was genuinely barred from his country for a doctrine the dictionary judges to be error, and the dictionary does not pretend otherwise; what it honours is the work he did with the years, which was honest, patient and of lasting use to men who disagreed with him.

The principle to recover is that the believer's true citizenship is elsewhere, and that this is to govern conduct rather than to produce melancholy. Hebrews draws the inference from the patriarchs' own words, “For they that say such things declare plainly that they seek a country” (Heb 11:14). The exiles by Babylon's rivers asked the harder question, “How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?” (Psa 137:4). And Peter makes the standing of a stranger the ground of a practical charge: “I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts” (1Pe 2:11).

pos: n. (German superintendent of the Swedish church, c. 1500–1553; set over the bishops by Gustav Vasa in 1539)
etymology: From German Norman, the northman; the given name Georg, Greek georgos, a husbandman.
biblical_def: Georg Norman was a German scholar, a pupil of Melanchthon, whom Gustav Vasa brought to Sweden as tutor to his sons and then, in 1539, appointed ordinarius and superintendent over the whole Swedish church, with authority above the bishops and answerable only to the king. The aim was a reformation on the north German model, administered from the court: visitations were ordered, church property inventoried and much of it removed, bishops reduced to royal officers. The Swedish clergy and the Dalecarlian peasants resisted, the archbishop Laurentius Petri held his ground, and by 1543 Norman had been quietly moved to civil administration, where he served usefully until his death. The dictionary records him because his office is the clearest Scandinavian instance of the state assuming an authority in the church that Scripture does not give it. The priests who withstood King Uzziah said the necessary sentence: “It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD” (2Ch 26:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a superintendent as one who has the oversight and charge of something; to trespass as to transgress, to violate a law; and an office as a particular duty or charge conferred by authority.
webster_full: SUPERINTENDENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.
TRESPASS, v.i. To transgress; to violate any known rule of duty; to commit any offense against law or morality.
OFFICE, n. [L. officium.] A particular duty, charge or trust conferred by public authority and for a public purpose.
SANCTUARY, n. [L. sanctuarium.] A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple, the holy of holies.
scriptures: And they withstood Uzziah the king, and said unto him, It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, that are consecrated to burn incense: go out of the sanctuary; for thou hast trespassed; neither shall it be for thine honour from the LORD God.

And Samuel said to Saul, Thou hast done foolishly: thou hast not kept the commandment of the LORD thy God, which he commanded thee: for now would the LORD have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever.
Heb 5:4
And no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron.
Num 18:7

Therefore thou and thy sons with thee shall keep your priest's office for every thing of the altar, and within the vail; and ye shall serve: I have given your priest's office unto you as a service of gift: and the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death.
corruption_summary: Melanchthon's pupil, made superintendent over the Swedish bishops by Gustav Vasa in 1539; the office failed and was abandoned by 1543.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is Erastianism, the doctrine that the civil power governs the church, which the Reformation sometimes resisted and sometimes embraced according to the needs of the prince. Norman's office was its boldest northern form: a royal officer placed over bishops, with the visitation and the property in his hands. The dictionary rejects it, and rejects equally the Roman error in the other direction, a church claiming jurisdiction over princes. Each sphere has its own authority and neither may assume the other's.

The principle to recover is that sacred office is conferred by God and is not at the disposal of the state. Samuel told Saul what came of acting the priest, “Thou hast done foolishly: thou hast not kept the commandment of the LORD thy God” (1Sa 13:13). Hebrews makes the call the only entrance, since “no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron” (Heb 5:4). And the law guarded the boundary with the severest sanction it had: “the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death” (Num 18:7).

pos: n. (bishop of Vasteras, 1581–1646; founder of the Swedish gymnasium and of the parish catechetical examination)
etymology: Latinised Swedish Rudbeck, from a place name; the suffix -ius a scholar's Latin form.
biblical_def: Johannes Rudbeckius was the greatest Swedish churchman of the seventeenth century and the reason Sweden became a literate country before any other in Europe. Professor at Uppsala, chaplain to Gustavus Adolphus, and from 1619 bishop of Vasteras, he founded in his diocese the first Swedish gymnasium, a school for girls, a hospital, a house for the poor, a printing press and a diocesan library, and he established the husförhör, the household examination, under which the parish minister visited every home annually and tested every member of it, servants and children included, on the catechism and on reading. Church law made the ability to read a condition of communion and of marriage. Within a century Swedish literacy was near universal. The dictionary records him because he turned a doctrine into a habit. “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to train as to educate, to teach, to form by instruction and practice; a gymnasium as a place of exercise, and in Germany a school for classical learning; and to catechise as to instruct by asking questions.
webster_full: TRAIN, v.t. To draw along; to educate; to teach; to form by instruction or practice; to bring up.
GYMNASIUM, n. [Gr.] A place where athletic exercises are performed; in Germany, a school or seminary for classical learning.
CATECHISE, v.t. [Gr.] To instruct by asking questions and correcting the answers; to examine or instruct by questions.
EXAMINATION, n. [L. examinatio.] The act of examining; a careful search or inquiry with a view to discover truth.
scriptures: Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them;
Deu 6:6
And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart:
Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears.
corruption_summary: Bishop of Vasteras; founded the first Swedish gymnasium and the annual household examination that made Sweden literate.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the reduction of Christian instruction to whatever a family will volunteer for, with the result that it happens in the few homes that were going to do it anyway. Rudbeckius did not leave it to willingness. He made the visitation annual, the examination universal within the parish, and reading a requirement for the Lord's Table and for marriage. Such a system can certainly harden into formality, and in Sweden it eventually did; but a formality that leaves a nation able to read its Bible is a better inheritance than a sincerity that leaves it illiterate.

The principle to recover is that instruction is to be continuous, domestic and personally applied. Paul grounds Timothy's perseverance in what he has learned and in whom he learned it from: “But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of” (2Ti 3:14). Moses requires the words to be lodged in the teacher first, “And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart” (Deu 6:6). And Paul's own method at Ephesus was individual and relentless: he “ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears” (Act 20:31).
